rv.q: The Greeks were all about agōn — argument — and this Antigone is at its hottest when Ziegler drives into the ancient form and pits two unstoppable forces against each other.
Ms. Ziegler’s play concludes on a moving note that is starkly brutal, and bloody, in keeping with classical tragedy.
Her vision is promising, but in need of revision.
I admire the concept of tying reproductive politics to 'Antigone' but not the way the play keeps trampling over its own ideas.
Susannah Perkins is riveting as Antigone in Anna Ziegler's new take on Sophocles' classic.

The production, buoyed by powerful performances and a depiction of a heart-felt duel between a beloved if obstinate uncle and niece, is thoroughly compelling and gives us plenty to chew on as we make the connection between the mythological past and the current state of things.
Her “Antigone” doesn’t have the ghoulish fascination of the original; however, as depicted here, birth and abortion can be far more scary.

Its flaws notwithstanding, there’s little question this “Antigone” provides serious food for thought that should prepare us for the difficult personal and political decisions that lie ahead for all of us, regardless of age or gender.
“Antigone (This Play I Read in High School)” doesn’t always work.

But if the first intervention gives us a new lens on the stakes, the second blunts and muddies them, turning Antigone’s searing and tragic outcome into a gentler, almost hopeful story about coming to terms with motherhood and motherlessness.
Even her title gets in the way as this is not the play we read in high school.
The show’s ambition to make Sophocles’s heroic insurgent an of-the-moment avatar for bodily autonomy and women's rights cracks under its over-literal, overwrought writing.
Powerful and gripping, this modern Antigone is laser‑focused on the cost—and the moral necessity—of refusing to acquiesce to power.
And in this electrifying production at Theater, it rings louder than ever.
It’s a far more urgent work that resurfaces one of Western literature’s first female revels, and gives her a new and vital sense of purpose.
The cast mostly delivers, but the allegory wobbles.
No amount of smart design or thoughtful direction can fix a playwright who does not trust her own vision enough to let the drama speak for itself.

cn.t: Ziegler's feminist riff on Sophocles draws mixed reactions: some critics praise its timely abortion rights focus and sharp wit, while others find it overly explanatory and lacking dramatic conflict, with performances generally admired.

vr.q: I enjoyed this play quite a bit despite its occasionally flawed execution.
